transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-13
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Liam Patel (NimbusFin SRE), Priya Shah (NimbusFin ML Eng), Jordan Kim (NimbusFin PM)
Shared artifacts: https://redwood.internal/velocity/poc/benchmarks (shared during call), security pack (link shared after)

Summary:
Quick sync on this week's throughput numbers; discussed continuous batching adjustments, concurrency targets, queueing strategy for tail latency, and next steps to validate steady-state economics. Agreed on a 6-hour run and to exchange configs/trace artifacts.

Topics covered:
- Results review from last week's 2-hour burst tests
- Adjustments to continuous batching window and max tokens per batch
- Concurrency target tradeoffs (p50 vs p99 latency)
- Queue depth shaping and backpressure behavior during spikes
- KV-cache warmup patterns and cold-start mitigation
- Security/SSO and KMS clarifications

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: ok everybody can hear me? great, thanks for joining the velocity P O C weekly, we've got about 55 minutes, lots to cover. Diego and I will run through the numbers then hand off to Liam and Priya for the next steps.
[00:22] Diego: hey all, quick note — I pulled the 2h burst run from last thursday, the config was continuous-batching window 25ms, max-batch-tokens 1024, concurrency target 24. i know you tried the 48 concurrency last week so i kept both for comparison.
[00:41] Liam: yep, we saw higher throughput with 48 but the 99 th jumped, like from 210 to 410 ms which is rough for the product path, so we pulled back.
[01:05] Priya: right, that 99 tail was the problem. also i think the batcher had a small bug where short prompts were being padded leading to larger effective batch sizes, not sure if that is a redwood issue or our preprocessing.
[01:30] Diego: mm-hmm, there was a padding policy we left permissive for the test. i can flip it to strict and re-run, that should reduce unnecessary tokens per batch.
[01:48] Jordan: just to clarify, our key success metric for this pilot is cost per 1k responses with p99 latency under 600ms for interactive flows.
[02:10] Maya: good, that's explicit. so goal: cost/1k and p99 < 600ms. noted.
[02:30] Diego: quick numbers from the chart — with 24 concurrency and window 25ms we averaged 1.2k rps with p50 110ms p99 270ms, with 48 concurrency that went to 2.1k rps but p99 to 410ms. with padding fix expected to drop that p99 maybe 30-60ms.
[03:05] Liam: what's the CPU/GPU occupancy look like at those settings? we don't want OOMs or saturating kernels.
[03:20] Diego: GPU utilization sits around 78% at 24 concurrency and 92% at 48 — memory footprint increases with batch tokens so there's a hard cap. we saw a couple of outlier time slices where queue depth spiked to 160ms wait.
[03:49] Priya: is queue depth the server-side request queue or the batcher waiting window? we've got both in our head.
[04:00] Diego: good call — i mean server-side queueing. the batcher waiting window is the 25ms. queue depth spike is from upstream traffic shaping; during the replay we had bursts that pushed many short requests causing the server queue to form.
[04:22] Jordan: can we smooth upstream to avoid those spikes? product can throttle slightly but want to understand fallback behavior if it still happens.
[04:35] Maya: Redwood provides burst capacity/fallbacks; we can route to a cheaper model variant temporarily, but that changes quality. another option is queue shaping and jittered retry from client side.
[04:56] Liam: fallback's OK as a last resort, but prefer stable p99. Also, how does KV-cache warmup factor in? during the 2h tests we saw first 10 minutes much lower throughput.
[05:20] Diego: KV-cache warms over warm prefixes — for your workload the session affinity helps. suggestion: preload common prefixes in a warmup run and then start the steady-state test. that'll shave the initial ramp.
[05:40] Priya: we can do that — we'll provide the top-100 prompt shapes.
[06:00] Maya: excellent. quick security note — i heard previously you asked about KMS key hold and SSO for the private pilot?
[06:10] Liam: yes, just to confirm, for now staging is fine but we'll need SSO and customer-managed KMS once we move to private. can you share your SOC2 and encryption details?
[06:30] Maya: yes, i'll share SOC2, ISO and the KMS whitepaper after the call. i'll schedule a security follow-up with our compliance lead.
[06:45] Jordan: awesome.
[07:00] Diego: back to tuning — we also tried reducing continuous-batching window to 10ms to see lower latency but that dropped throughput by ~18%. tradeoff there.
[07:20] Priya: did that change the average tokens per batch?
[07:32] Diego: yes, average tokens per batch decreased from ~6.3 to ~3.9. that reduced model efficiency. so if your workload is short prompts, very small windows hurt QPS.
[07:51] Liam: what's your recommendation for short prompts heavy workloads?
[08:00] Diego: try hybrid: small window (10ms) but a slightly higher max-batch-tokens cap and use adaptive batching — increase window when model sees many short prompts to aggregate more. we've got an adaptive script we can enable.
[08:22] Priya: adaptive sounds promising, are there stability risks? i.e., oscillation during bursty traffic?
[08:35] Diego: potential for oscillation, so we add hysteresis and rate-limited adjustments. i've included thresholds in the config we plan to send.
[08:50] Jordan: curious — how do you test these in dedicated vs hosted? anything different for dedicated?
[09:00] Diego: main differences are scheduling and queue guarantees. dedicated gives you reserved capacity so less noisy neighbors and more predictable batching behavior. hosted has more dynamic placement but Redwood's routing stabilizes it. for piloting, your staging is on a dedicated-like pool.
[09:20] Liam: okay good. next i want to talk fallback policy logic — can we set a quality guardrail percentage? e.g., only fallback if less than 3% of requests would degrade quality beyond threshold.
[09:38] Maya: yes we can tie fallbacks to quality metrics. that requires instrumentation — we'll need your eval prompts so the platform can measure quality delta.
[09:52] Priya: sending top-200 eval prompts after this call.
[10:05] Diego: small aside — we saw one spike where batcher latency spiked due to a serialization overhead when compressing KV entries, that was a library mismatch. we patched it in our test image.
[10:25] Liam: good catch. did that affect memory?
[10:30] Diego: minimal, just CPU during compress. fixed in image redwood/serve:v1.14.2-test.
[10:45] Jordan: any thoughts on concurrency target? are we leaning to 24 or 36?
[10:55] Diego: recommended target is 30 for mixed prompt lengths with adaptive batching and strict padding. gives good throughput while keeping p99 under 400ms in our sim.
[11:12] Priya: let's test 30 then.
[11:18] Liam: ok but we want an A/B between 24 and 30 to understand cost delta, can we run both in parallel traffic replay?
[11:30] Diego: yes, we can run two pools and compare. i'll prepare a charting template.
[11:42] Maya: timeline wise, what's feasible this week?
[11:50] Diego: i can share config today; if Liam kicks off the steady-state run tomorrow, we can have initial results within 48 hours, full 6h run by tuesday next week.
[12:05] Jordan: sounds good.
[12:10] Maya: quick security recap — i'll post SOC2 and KMS notes and set up that SSO follow-up.
[12:18] Liam: appreciate it.
[12:24] Diego: any blockers on our side?
[12:30] Priya: none, just need the exact batcher config comments so we can mirror it in infra.
[12:38] Diego: i'll annotate the config with comments about expected latency/throughput tradeoffs per param.
[12:50] Jordan: can you also include the fallback policy JSON snippet? even if it's pseudo, helps product review.
[12:58] Maya: yes we'll include that.
[13:10] Diego: another note — prefix caching: we suggest a 5-minute TTL for your workload to keep useful keys in memory without causing stale user-state exposure.
[13:25] Liam: 5 minutes sounds fine.
[13:30] Priya: question on billing model: if we run dedicated pools and use burst capacity will billing be predictable?
[13:40] Maya: dedicated has a reserved-cost plus burst overage; we can model costs for 3 scenarios: steady, bursty, and hybrid. i'll send a simple spreadsheet.
[13:54] Jordan: okay cool.
[14:05] Diego: going to call out the run parameters we'll send in the notes: concurrency A/ B (24 vs 30), continuous-batch window 25ms, strict padding enabled, max-batch-tokens 1024, adaptive-batching enabled with hysteresis 10%.
[14:25] Priya: perfect.
[14:35] Liam: one more thing — can you include a short how-to on client-side jittered retries? in our infra we can add that quickly.
[14:46] Diego: yes, short snippet and recommended backoff schedule.
[15:00] Maya: alright let's jump to open questions from customer. Liam?
[15:06] Liam: none beyond what we discussed.
[15:10] Jordan: timeline question — if the steady-state run shows p99 under 600ms and cost target met, what's next for enterprise?
[15:20] Maya: next is security review sign-off, then we move staging to a dedicated reserve and start a longer pilot with SSO and KMS. sales will draft the pilot SOW.
[15:35] Jordan: ok good.
[15:40] Diego: quick note on metrics collection — make sure your agent includes model-token and wall-time per response so we can compute true per-token cost.
[15:52] Priya: will do.
[16:00] Maya: any other items?
[16:04] silence
[16:10] Maya: ok wrap up — recap of next steps: Diego shares config + fallback snippet (today), Maya shares security pack and schedules SSO follow-up (by 2026-10-16), Liam runs 6-hour steady-state (by 2026-10-20), Priya sends traces and eval prompts (by 2026-10-18).
[16:35] Jordan: thanks everyone.
[16:40] Maya: thanks — we'll follow up in the ticket and update the shared drive.
[16:50] call ended

Recap / explicit next steps:
- Diego to upload annotated batcher config + fallback JSON snippet (shared link in chat) — due 2026-10-15.
- Liam to run 6h steady-state with KV warmup and provide logs/traces — due 2026-10-20.
- Priya to send 95/99 latency traces and top prompts — due 2026-10-18.
- Maya to share SOC2/ISO/KMS docs and schedule compliance call — due 2026-10-16.

Notes about transcription: multiple speakers and occasional ASR errors (e.g., "kay vee cache" for KV cache, some product names slightly mis-transcribed).
